es across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

### Summary

Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund.

State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.

Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.

KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. A California proposition to fund medical research is creating strange alliances on both sides
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 15, 2026
Scientists from UCSF, UC Berkeley and Stanford, community members and state Sen. Scott Wiener rally in San Francisco on May 16, 2025 to support a ballot measure to offset scientific research cuts. That measure will appear on the 2028 ballot.
Jessica Christian/S.F. Chronicle
A ballot measure that would raise billions for health research is drawing some unlikely foes, in a race that has already forged a handful of atypical alliances.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to borrow $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, presented as a way of backfilling some of the widespread cuts to federal research funding by President Donald Trump.
The funds would be split between an unnamed University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions, and half of the funds are earmarked to support research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.

But the measure’s cast of supporters and detractors are not quite so clear-cut.
On the Yes on Prop 38 side, California’s Republican and Democratic parties are in rare agreement, both backing a yes vote on the billion-dollar bond measure.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also said he plans to vote for the measure in November (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), joining a list of health and research advocacy groups including the Parkinson’s Foundation, the ALS Association and the American Nurses Association of California.
On the opposite side, the No on Prop 38 campaign has amassed its own eclectic — albeit much smaller — group of backers. The progressive League of Women Voters of California and Common Cause California find themselves in rare company with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a conservative-aligned anti-tax group that opposes virtually every bond measure.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
And this week, the measure attracted a new front of opposition from a trio of current and former California state parks professionals and officials.
That might prompt a reasonable question: What do parks even have to do with a health bond?
Ruth Coleman, executive director of trade organization California Parks Hospitality Association, joined the No on Prop 38 campaign to decry the ballot measure’s possible impacts on other state funding priorities, including public parks.
“Any measure that increases our bonded indebtedness increases pressure on programs like state parks,” Coleman said at a Tuesday news conference.
Coleman is a former director of California State Parks and a former fiscal analyst in the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s nonpartisan fiscal and policy analysis organization. She warned that because the bond’s repayment takes priority, it could cut into the state’s ability to pay for other programs in leaner years.

Article continues below this ad
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the measure will cost the state $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years in bond repayment.
Coleman clarified she doesn’t think that bonds themselves are bad, and that they have helped fund public parks in recent years. She and two other former parks professionals, however, warned that funding for public spaces could fall on the cutting room floor if the bond passes. In economic downturns, Coleman said legislators have looked at parks funding as “a nice to have, but not a must have.”
In 2024, California voters approved Prop 4 to authorize $10 billion in bonds for projects to reduce climate risks and impacts, and committed $190 million to the statewide parks program.
As of Wednesday, the No campaign did not count any organizations representing parks, conservation or the environment among its backers.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on 38 campaign, said in a statement that the ballot measure would not compete with other priorities, as it is “designed to pay for itself.”

Prop 38 requires that the institutes receiving the funds try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research, and that 10% of any related revenues go to the state. According to a report by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, that potential revenue source is uncertain, and dependent on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments, and how successful they are.
Researchers from Doudna Labs discussed the ramifications of National Institutes of Health research cuts with members of Congress in Berkeley on Feb. 21, 2025.
Colin Peck/For the S.F. Chronicle It’s not a new bond structure — two semi-recent ballot measures took similar approaches to scientific research.
In 2004, voters approved Prop 71, a $3 billion bond measure to fund stem cell therapy research with the aim of bolstering critical studies and therapies for rare and complex diseases. A 2018 investigation by the Chronicle (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/) found the measure failed to reach its promises of paying the state back in billions of discovery-related royalties.
In 2020, voters approved Prop 14 to infuse another $5.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research.

Swanson said Prop 38 will provide billions in “vitally needed funding to advance breakthrough immunology research to develop life-saving treatments and cures for the most persistent and debilitating diseases.”
The measure has sparked criticism for its hyper-specific language that appears to ensure half the billion-dollar funds go directly to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy, the sole institution that meets the measure’s criteria. The ballot measure’s proponent and largest financial backer, philanthropist Gary Michelson, is a co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
The opposition camp is headed by Robert Kaplan, a senior scholar at the Clinical Excellence Research Center at Stanford School of Medicine and David Panush, a veteran legislative adviser and president of consulting firm California Health Policy Strategies. They object to the use of bond funds to support scientific research rather than general budgeting processes, and criticize it as inflexible and lacking transparency.
Panush has called the measure an outrageous attempt to use the ballot initiative process to fund Michelson’s institute. The California chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America made the same point to explain its opposition, calling the measure “naked self-dealing” in its voter guide.
Just a few weeks out from the Nov. 3 election, the Yes on 38 campaign’s coffers sit at a dramatic advantage, outraising the opposition campaign by the millions. Bolstered by multiple million-dollar contributions by Michelson, the Yes campaign boasts more than $50 million raised, while the No campaign hasn’t yet topped the $10,000 mark as of Wednesday.
The controversial requirements stand in stark contrast with a competing science bond ballot measure that failed to secure a spot on the November ballot.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, introduced Senate Bill 895 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) in the first few weeks of the legislative session, which began as a $23 billion bond measure designed to backfill Trump cuts to science and health research. After months of debate and a significant slash down to $12 billion, the measure appeared poised for the November ballot. But in obscure last-minute negotiations involving top Democratic leadership and the governor’s office, it was punted to 2028. The bond amount was also cut down even further, to $7.5 billion.
In his ballot statement, Kaplan pointed to Wiener’s bond as a better alternative to Prop 38, which proposes creating a new state agency to distribute and manage the funds, and would be able to meet changing funding and research needs rather than committing the funds to specific institutions and research areas indefinitely.
Erik Mebust, spokesperson for Wiener, said he is not taking a position on Prop 38.
Trump last year froze more than $600 million to fund UC research that a judge eventually restored months later. The National Institutes of Health under Trump also scaled back the number of new research grants it funded in 2025 to 3,900 from 5,000 the year before under President Joe Biden.
Grants for Alzheimer’s disease research were cut in half and new cancer research grants dropped by 23%, according to federal data.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.

NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.

A California proposition to fund medical research is creating strange alliances on both sides
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 15, 2026
Scientists from UCSF, UC Berkeley and Stanford, community members and state Sen. Scott Wiener rally in San Francisco on May 16, 2025 to support a ballot measure to offset scientific research cuts. That measure will appear on the 2028 ballot.
Jessica Christian/S.F. Chronicle
A ballot measure that would raise billions for health research is drawing some unlikely foes, in a race that has already forged a handful of atypical alliances.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to borrow $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, presented as a way of backfilling some of the widespread cuts to federal research funding by President Donald Trump.
The funds would be split between an unnamed University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions, and half of the funds are earmarked to support research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.

But the measure’s cast of supporters and detractors are not quite so clear-cut.
On the Yes on Prop 38 side, California’s Republican and Democratic parties are in rare agreement, both backing a yes vote on the billion-dollar bond measure.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also said he plans to vote for the measure in November (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), joining a list of health and research advocacy groups including the Parkinson’s Foundation, the ALS Association and the American Nurses Association of California.
On the opposite side, the No on Prop 38 campaign has amassed its own eclectic — albeit much smaller — group of backers. The progressive League of Women Voters of California and Common Cause California find themselves in rare company with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a conservative-aligned anti-tax group that opposes virtually every bond measure.

And this week, the measure attracted a new front of opposition from a trio of current and former California state parks professionals and officials.
That might prompt a reasonable question: What do parks even have to do with a health bond?
Ruth Coleman, executive director of trade organization California Parks Hospitality Association, joined the No on Prop 38 campaign to decry the ballot measure’s possible impacts on other state funding priorities, including public parks.
“Any measure that increases our bonded indebtedness increases pressure on programs like state parks,” Coleman said at a Tuesday news conference.
Coleman is a former director of California State Parks and a former fiscal analyst in the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s nonpartisan fiscal and policy analysis organization. She warned that because the bond’s repayment takes priority, it could cut into the state’s ability to pay for other programs in leaner years.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the measure will cost the state $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years in bond repayment.
Coleman clarified she doesn’t think that bonds themselves are bad, and that they have helped fund public parks in recent years. She and two other former parks professionals, however, warned that funding for public spaces could fall on the cutting room floor if the bond passes. In economic downturns, Coleman said legislators have looked at parks funding as “a nice to have, but not a must have.”
In 2024, California voters approved Prop 4 to authorize $10 billion in bonds for projects to reduce climate risks and impacts, and committed $190 million to the statewide parks program.

She warned that because the bond’s repayment takes priority, it could cut into the state’s ability to pay for other programs in leaner years.

I'm looking at the PPIC numbers for Prop 38: 57% yes and 41% no as of October 16–22. Among the groups, Democrats slipped from 76% to 70% support, Republicans rose from 23% to 37%, and independents stayed about even, which nudged the overall figure from 55 to 57. Next I'm turning to the editorial opposition, starting with the SF Chronicle's harsh description of the measure.

I'm now checking which groups oppose the measure beyond the editorial boards, since the SF Chronicle piece mentions "unlikely foes." I'll look at the article and the IGS endorsements list to see who is on each side.

A California proposition to fund medical research is creating strange alliances on both sides
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 15, 2026
Scientists from UCSF, UC Berkeley and Stanford, community members and state Sen. Scott Wiener rally in San Francisco on May 16, 2025 to support a ballot measure to offset scientific research cuts. That measure will appear on the 2028 ballot.
Jessica Christian/S.F. Chronicle
A ballot measure that would raise billions for health research is drawing some unlikely foes, in a race that has already forged a handful of atypical alliances.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to borrow $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, presented as a way of backfilling some of the widespread cuts to federal research funding by President Donald Trump.
The funds would be split between an unnamed University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions, and half of the funds are earmarked to support research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But the measure’s cast of supporters and detractors are not quite so clear-cut.
On the Yes on Prop 38 side, California’s Republican and Democratic parties are in rare agreement, both backing a yes vote on the billion-dollar bond measure.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also said he plans to vote for the measure in November (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), joining a list of health and research advocacy groups including the Parkinson’s Foundation, the ALS Association and the American Nurses Association of California.
On the opposite side, the No on Prop 38 campaign has amassed its own eclectic — albeit much smaller — group of backers. The progressive League of Women Voters of California and Common Cause California find themselves in rare company with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a conservative-aligned anti-tax group that opposes virtually every bond measure.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
And this week, the measure attracted a new front of opposition from a trio of current and former California state parks professionals and officials.
That might prompt a reasonable question: What do parks even have to do with a health bond?
Ruth Coleman, executive director of trade organization California Parks Hospitality Association, joined the No on Prop 38 campaign to decry the ballot measure’s possible impacts on other state funding priorities, including public parks.
“Any measure that increases our bonded indebtedness increases pressure on programs like state parks,” Coleman said at a Tuesday news conference.
Coleman is a former director of California State Parks and a former fiscal analyst in the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s nonpartisan fiscal and policy analysis organization. She warned that because the bond’s repayment takes priority, it could cut into the state’s ability to pay for other programs in leaner years.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the measure will cost the state $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years in bond repayment.
Coleman clarified she doesn’t think that bonds themselves are bad, and that they have helped fund public parks in recent years. She and two other former parks professionals, however, warned that funding for public spaces could fall on the cutting room floor if the bond passes. In economic downturns, Coleman said legislators have looked at parks funding as “a nice to have, but not a must have.”
In 2024, California voters approved Prop 4 to authorize $10 billion in bonds for projects to reduce climate risks and impacts, and committed $190 million to the statewide parks program.
As of Wednesday, the No campaign did not count any organizations representing parks, conservation or the environment among its backers.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on 38 campaign, said in a statement that the ballot measure would not compete with other priorities, as it is “designed to pay for itself.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 requires that the institutes receiving the funds try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research, and that 10% of any related revenues go to the state. According to a report by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, that potential revenue source is uncertain, and dependent on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments, and how successful they are.
Researchers from Doudna Labs discussed the ramifications of National Institutes of Health research cuts with members of Congress in Berkeley on Feb. 21, 2025.
Colin Peck/For the S.F. Chronicle It’s not a new bond structure — two semi-recent ballot measures took similar approaches to scientific research.
In 2004, voters approved Prop 71, a $3 billion bond measure to fund stem cell therapy research with the aim of bolstering critical studies and therapies for rare and complex diseases. A 2018 investigation by the Chronicle (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/) found the measure failed to reach its promises of paying the state back in billions of discovery-related royalties.
In 2020, voters approved Prop 14 to infuse another $5.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Swanson said Prop 38 will provide billions in “vitally needed funding to advance breakthrough immunology research to develop life-saving treatments and cures for the most persistent and debilitating diseases.”
The measure has sparked criticism for its hyper-specific language that appears to ensure half the billion-dollar funds go directly to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy, the sole institution that meets the measure’s criteria. The ballot measure’s proponent and largest financial backer, philanthropist Gary Michelson, is a co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
The opposition camp is headed by Robert Kaplan, a senior scholar at the Clinical Excellence Research Center at Stanford School of Medicine and David Panush, a veteran legislative adviser and president of consulting firm California Health Policy Strategies. They object to the use of bond funds to support scientific research rather than general budgeting processes, and criticize it as inflexible and lacking transparency.
Panush has called the measure an outrageous attempt to use the ballot initiative process to fund Michelson’s institute. The California chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America made the same point to explain its opposition, calling the measure “naked self-dealing” in its voter guide.
Just a few weeks out from the Nov. 3 election, the Yes on 38 campaign’s coffers sit at a dramatic advantage, outraising the opposition campaign by the millions. Bolstered by multiple million-dollar contributions by Michelson, the Yes campaign boasts more than $50 million raised, while the No campaign hasn’t yet topped the $10,000 mark as of Wednesday.
The controversial requirements stand in stark contrast with a competing science bond ballot measure that failed to secure a spot on the November ballot.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, introduced Senate Bill 895 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) in the first few weeks of the legislative session, which began as a $23 billion bond measure designed to backfill Trump cuts to science and health research. After months of debate and a significant slash down to $12 billion, the measure appeared poised for the November ballot. But in obscure last-minute negotiations involving top Democratic leadership and the governor’s office, it was punted to 2028. The bond amount was also cut down even further, to $7.5 billion.
In his ballot statement, Kaplan pointed to Wiener’s bond as a better alternative to Prop 38, which proposes creating a new state agency to distribute and manage the funds, and would be able to meet changing funding and research needs rather than committing the funds to specific institutions and research areas indefinitely.
Erik Mebust, spokesperson for Wiener, said he is not taking a position on Prop 38.
Trump last year froze more than $600 million to fund UC research that a judge eventually restored months later. The National Institutes of Health under Trump also scaled back the number of new research grants it funded in 2025 to 3,900 from 5,000 the year before under President Joe Biden.
Grants for Alzheimer’s disease research were cut in half and new cancer research grants dropped by 23%, according to federal data.

I'm going through the endorsements for Prop 38. Most of the newspapers, including the Bay Area News Group, Press-Enterprise, OC Register, Sacramento Bee, San Diego Union-Tribune, SF Bay Guardian, SF Chronicle, and probably Santa Rosa Press-Democrat, are against it, while the LA Times has no endorsement. On the non-profit side, California Church IMPACT is for it, and the California Pan-Ethnic Health Network is against it, with CalTax still to check.

Both major parties back it, while every major newspaper opposes it. The yes side has a large money edge and PPIC polling sits at 57-41, which points toward passage. I'm also weighing how past measures with that kind of spending and editorial opposition have fared, and how the crowded ballot might affect voters.

I'm checking the earlier polling comparisons: the late PPIC numbers for past bond measures, and whether those polls tended to overstate or understate final support.

I'm now checking how PPIC's late polls for earlier bond measures compared with final results. Prop 13 in 2020 and the 2018 bonds like Props 1, 2, 3, and 4 show polls sometimes landing close to the result and sometimes well off, so I'm noting where the gaps were largest.

I'm weighing PPIC's 57-41 lead against typical late shifts toward "no," which would still leave it passing around 52-54%. I also want to check for other polls from late October and any post-election results, since the page may have been fetched before those came out.

I'm now looking for any post-election coverage of Prop 38, searching for results that might confirm whether voters approved or rejected the immunology bond.

1. We asked the No on Prop. 38 campaign why voters should reject the measure
https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/
Californians are being asked to vote 'yes' or 'no' on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research.
Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs.
Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting 'yes' means California can borrow the money.
Voting 'no' means it can't.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it's endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure's criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion.
Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.

# On Your November Ballot: Prop 38 Would Allocate $8.4 Billion to Immunology and Immunotherapy Funding
**By Austin Gage, California Black Media**
California voters will decide in November whether Proposition (Prop) 38 should authorize substantial state funding for immunology and immunotherapy research.
The initiative would fund immunology and immunotherapy research aimed at harnessing the body’s immune system to develop new treatments, medical procedures and potential cures for diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease.
More specifically, Prop 38, **titled the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative**, is split into three main components that would go into effect if passed.
First, the initiative would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to support immunology and immunotherapy research.
At least half of the bond proceeds, or $4.2 billion, would be dedicated exclusively to research.

I'm also weighing how past measures with that kind of spending and editorial opposition have fared, and how the crowded ballot might affect voters.

I'm checking the earlier polling comparisons: the late PPIC numbers for past bond measures, and whether those polls tended to overstate or understate final support.

November 3, 2026
California voters are casting ballots in races for governor and the state’s 52 US House seats. Four House races could be competitive, according to ratings from the Cook Political Report (https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings). In California’s open gubernatorial race, Democrat Xavier Becerra faces Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2026-steve-hilton-weekend-interview/). Bloomberg News is also tracking eight key ballot measures across the Golden State, including a one-time wealth tax on billionaires and changes to the state’s environmental quality legislation.
California voters approved a ballot measure in 2025 that allows the state (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-04/supreme-court-allows-new-california-voting-map-for-midterms) to use a congressional map drawn by the legislature. The new congressional map supported by Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom is intended to increase the share of Democratic-leaning House districts.

US Election 2026 California Election Results
November 3, 2026
California voters are casting ballots in races for governor and the state’s 52 US House seats. Four House races could be competitive, according to ratings from the Cook Political Report (https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings). In California’s open gubernatorial race, Democrat Xavier Becerra faces Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2026-steve-hilton-weekend-interview/). Bloomberg News is also tracking eight key ballot measures across the Golden State, including a one-time wealth tax on billionaires and changes to the state’s environmental quality legislation.
California voters approved a ballot measure in 2025 that allows the state (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-04/supreme-court-allows-new-california-voting-map-for-midterms) to use a congressional map drawn by the legislature. The new congressional map supported by Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom is intended to increase the share of Democratic-leaning House districts.

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
