CALIFORNIA DECIDES | Proposition Lab
PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research

Key Questions

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.
For help choosing where to trade ballot measures, compare election prediction apps (https://defirate.com/prediction-markets/politics/) for proposition coverage, fees and access.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.
For help choosing where to trade ballot measures, compare election prediction apps (https://defirate.com/prediction-markets/politics/) for proposition coverage, fees and access.

“ No on Proposition 38 ”

Knock LA
“ This is a total corruption of the ballot process and not how we should be funding medical research. Vote no. ”

The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
"The stakes are substantial," committee co-chair David Panush wrote.
"Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution.
Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds."
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a "campaign stunt to distract voters."

I'm weighing the evidence so far, and it leans clearly toward passage: the final PPIC poll has it at 57-41, up from 55 in September, and the Yes side has far outspent the No side on TV. I'm now starting to look at the opposition.

I'm checking the opposition side, which has editorial boards, good-government groups and a few notable names but no funded campaign, while prediction markets sit around 81% for passage. Past PPIC bond polls have tended to match or underestimate support, and the 2020 medical research bond passed narrowly despite a worse climate, so the main risk I'm weighing is the "self-dealing" narrative combined with the ballot label's wording.

The bonds in high-turnout November elections have tended to do well, and this year's electorate looks strongly Democratic. The measure's support splits along party lines in a way that a Democratic-leaning turnout should help, and the Prop 40 billionaire-tax debate might bleed into this one. Even so, the October poll already captured that environment and still showed 57%, so I'm landing around 80% for passage.

I'm going to check for any post-election coverage before settling on the forecast, trying a few phrasings like "Prop 38 passes" and "race call" to see whether results have come in.

I'm weighing the evidence so far, and it leans clearly toward passage: the final PPIC poll has it at 57-41, up from 55 in September, and the Yes side has far outspent the No side on TV. I'm now starting to look at the opposition.

I'm checking the opposition side, which has editorial boards, good-government groups and a few notable names but no funded campaign, while prediction markets sit around 81% for passage. Past PPIC bond polls have tended to match or underestimate support, and the 2020 medical research bond passed narrowly despite a worse climate, so the main risk I'm weighing is the "self-dealing" narrative combined with the ballot label's wording.

The bonds in high-turnout November elections have tended to do well, and this year's electorate looks strongly Democratic. The measure's support splits along party lines in a way that a Democratic-leaning turnout should help, and the Prop 40 billionaire-tax debate might bleed into this one. Even so, the October poll already captured that environment and still showed 57%, so I'm landing around 80% for passage.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
PATIENT ADVOCATES, DOCTORS, NURSES AND MEDICAL RESEARCHERS URGE YES ON PROP. 38
Leading patient advocates including the Alzheimer’s Association, Michael J. Fox Foundation, American Nurses Association\ California, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society and Prostate Cancer Foundation all urge YES on PROP. 38 because it could save your life and the life of someone you love.
“I was just weeks away from losing my life when a breakthrough immunotherapy gave me a second chance. Vote YES on PROP. 38 because every family facing a devastating diagnosis deserves this same hope.”
-Laurie Adami, Cancer Survivor and Patient Advocate, Los Angeles
YES ON PROP. 38-TO CURE AND PREVENT DISEASES THROUGH LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY RESEARCH
PROP. 38 accelerates development of breakthrough treatments and cures for the diseases that impact nearly every family. At least half of all funds are specifically dedicated to cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s research.
“Immunology harnesses the body’s immune system to detect and stop diseases. Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to prevent diseases including Parkinson’s, heart disease, diabetes and more.”
-Mark Davis, Ph.D., Member of the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine
“One in nine people over 65 are living with Alzheimer’s, but there are currently no effective cures. YES on PROP. 38 provides real promise to find treatments and cures for the millions of patients and their families living with Alzheimer’s and dementia.”
-Susan Disney Lord, Board Chair of Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
HELPS OFFSET FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS TO MEDICAL RESEARCH
Massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research at nonprofit research institutes and universities, delaying progress toward life-saving cures.
PROP. 38 creates a stable source of funding for breakthrough immunology research. All funds are dedicated exclusively to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes- helping California lead the nation in medical innovation, fostering collaboration among top scientists and universities, and creating tens of thousands of good-paying jobs.
“Immunotherapy is transforming the future of cancer care. PROP. 38 will help accelerate life-saving cures while strengthening California’s role as a global leader in medical innovation.”
-Gina Carithers, President and CEO, Prostate Cancer Foundation
LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS FOR CALIFORNIANS
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through PROP. 38 must be provided to California patients at a 20% DISCOUNT. Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will also reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save the state and families tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
PROP. 38 is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS. Ten percent of revenue from the licensing of successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the costs of the bond, including interest.
PROP. 38 also includes strict accountability requirements, including:
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses
Public Disclosure of Spending
Independent Financial Audits
For-profit corporations are not eligible for grant funding
YES ON PROP. 38: SUPPORTED BY DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES
• ALS Association • Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\California • Blood Cancer United • California Colorectal Cancer Coalition • Liver Coalition • Michael J. Fox Foundation • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • Parkinson Association of Northern California ... and many more.
YES on PROP. 38 could save your life and someone you love. Please, vote Yes.
www.YesOn38.com
Susan Disney Lord , Board Chair
Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
Eugene P. Brandon , Ph.D., Board of Trustees
ALS Association
Dr. Brian Shuch , M.D., Board of Directors Member
Kidney Cancer Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.

PROPOSITION 38
YES ON PROP. 38 IS VITALLY NEEDED FOR LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to cure and prevent diseases including Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, ALS and more.
MASSIVE FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS ARE THREATENING PROGRESS TOWARD LIFE-SAVING CURES
YES on 38 will ensure California universities and nonprofit research institutions can continue vitally needed immunology research to cure and prevent the most debilitating diseases.
“Immunology saved my life-I now live cancer-free, and it could save millions of other lives too.”
-Andrew Dale, Immunotherapy Patient and Cancer Survivor
YES ON 38 IS DESIGNED TO PAY FOR ITSELF-WITH NO COST TO TAXPAYERS
Ten percent (10%) of revenue from licensing immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset bond costs. These requirements are locked into this measure.
YES ON 38 MANDATES STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TRANSPARENCY
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses

Independent Financial Audits

Immunotherapies developed through Prop. 38 must be provided to California patients at 20% discount. Preventing and curing diseases will also save families and the state billions of dollars in long-term healthcare expenses.
DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES URGE YES ON 38
• Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\ California • ALS Association • Kidney Cancer Association • Melanoma Research Alliance • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research ... and many more.
Support Life-Saving Cures. Please Vote YES on 38.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
PATIENT ADVOCATES, DOCTORS, NURSES AND MEDICAL RESEARCHERS URGE YES ON PROP. 38
Leading patient advocates including the Alzheimer’s Association, Michael J. Fox Foundation, American Nurses Association\ California, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society and Prostate Cancer Foundation all urge YES on PROP. 38 because it could save your life and the life of someone you love.
“I was just weeks away from losing my life when a breakthrough immunotherapy gave me a second chance. Vote YES on PROP. 38 because every family facing a devastating diagnosis deserves this same hope.”
-Laurie Adami, Cancer Survivor and Patient Advocate, Los Angeles
YES ON PROP. 38-TO CURE AND PREVENT DISEASES THROUGH LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY RESEARCH
PROP. 38 accelerates development of breakthrough treatments and cures for the diseases that impact nearly every family. At least half of all funds are specifically dedicated to cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s research.
“Immunology harnesses the body’s immune system to detect and stop diseases. Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to prevent diseases including Parkinson’s, heart disease, diabetes and more.”
-Mark Davis, Ph.D., Member of the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine
“One in nine people over 65 are living with Alzheimer’s, but there are currently no effective cures. YES on PROP. 38 provides real promise to find treatments and cures for the millions of patients and their families living with Alzheimer’s and dementia.”
-Susan Disney Lord, Board Chair of Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
HELPS OFFSET FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS TO MEDICAL RESEARCH
Massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research at nonprofit research institutes and universities, delaying progress toward life-saving cures.
PROP. 38 creates a stable source of funding for breakthrough immunology research. All funds are dedicated exclusively to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes- helping California lead the nation in medical innovation, fostering collaboration among top scientists and universities, and creating tens of thousands of good-paying jobs.
“Immunotherapy is transforming the future of cancer care. PROP. 38 will help accelerate life-saving cures while strengthening California’s role as a global leader in medical innovation.”
-Gina Carithers, President and CEO, Prostate Cancer Foundation
LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS FOR CALIFORNIANS
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through PROP. 38 must be provided to California patients at a 20% DISCOUNT. Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will also reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save the state and families tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
PROP. 38 is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS. Ten percent of revenue from the licensing of successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the costs of the bond, including interest.
PROP. 38 also includes strict accountability requirements, including:
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses
Public Disclosure of Spending
Independent Financial Audits
For-profit corporations are not eligible for grant funding
YES ON PROP. 38: SUPPORTED BY DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES
• ALS Association • Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\California • Blood Cancer United • California Colorectal Cancer Coalition • Liver Coalition • Michael J. Fox Foundation • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • Parkinson Association of Northern California ... and many more.
YES on PROP. 38 could save your life and someone you love. Please, vote Yes.
www.YesOn38.com
Susan Disney Lord , Board Chair
Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
Eugene P. Brandon , Ph.D., Board of Trustees
ALS Association
Dr. Brian Shuch , M.D., Board of Directors Member
Kidney Cancer Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.

I'm also weighing whether the PPIC poll on Prop 38 overstates support, since respondents see only the title and summary, and low-information voters may lean yes on medical research measures.
