PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
PATIENT ADVOCATES, DOCTORS, NURSES AND MEDICAL RESEARCHERS URGE YES ON PROP. 38
Leading patient advocates including the Alzheimer’s Association, Michael J. Fox Foundation, American Nurses Association\ California, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society and Prostate Cancer Foundation all urge YES on PROP. 38 because it could save your life and the life of someone you love.
“I was just weeks away from losing my life when a breakthrough immunotherapy gave me a second chance. Vote YES on PROP. 38 because every family facing a devastating diagnosis deserves this same hope.”
-Laurie Adami, Cancer Survivor and Patient Advocate, Los Angeles
YES ON PROP. 38-TO CURE AND PREVENT DISEASES THROUGH LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY RESEARCH
PROP. 38 accelerates development of breakthrough treatments and cures for the diseases that impact nearly every family. At least half of all funds are specifically dedicated to cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s research.
“Immunology harnesses the body’s immune system to detect and stop diseases. Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to prevent diseases including Parkinson’s, heart disease, diabetes and more.”
-Mark Davis, Ph.D., Member of the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Medicine
“One in nine people over 65 are living with Alzheimer’s, but there are currently no effective cures. YES on PROP. 38 provides real promise to find treatments and cures for the millions of patients and their families living with Alzheimer’s and dementia.”
-Susan Disney Lord, Board Chair of Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
HELPS OFFSET FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS TO MEDICAL RESEARCH
Massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research at nonprofit research institutes and universities, delaying progress toward life-saving cures.
PROP. 38 creates a stable source of funding for breakthrough immunology research. All funds are dedicated exclusively to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes- helping California lead the nation in medical innovation, fostering collaboration among top scientists and universities, and creating tens of thousands of good-paying jobs.
“Immunotherapy is transforming the future of cancer care. PROP. 38 will help accelerate life-saving cures while strengthening California’s role as a global leader in medical innovation.”
-Gina Carithers, President and CEO, Prostate Cancer Foundation
LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS FOR CALIFORNIANS
Any cure or immunotherapy developed through PROP. 38 must be provided to California patients at a 20% DISCOUNT. Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will also reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save the state and families tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
PROP. 38 is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS. Ten percent of revenue from the licensing of successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the costs of the bond, including interest.
PROP. 38 also includes strict accountability requirements, including:
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses
Public Disclosure of Spending
Independent Financial Audits
For-profit corporations are not eligible for grant funding
YES ON PROP. 38: SUPPORTED BY DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES
• ALS Association • Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\California • Blood Cancer United • California Colorectal Cancer Coalition • Liver Coalition • Michael J. Fox Foundation • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • Parkinson Association of Northern California ... and many more.
YES on PROP. 38 could save your life and someone you love. Please, vote Yes.
www.YesOn38.com
Susan Disney Lord , Board Chair
Alzheimer’s Los Angeles
Eugene P. Brandon , Ph.D., Board of Trustees
ALS Association
Dr. Brian Shuch , M.D., Board of Directors Member
Kidney Cancer Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 38
YES ON PROP. 38 IS VITALLY NEEDED FOR LIFE-SAVING IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Today, breakthrough immunotherapies are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Promising research is underway to cure and prevent diseases including Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, ALS and more.
MASSIVE FEDERAL FUNDING CUTS ARE THREATENING PROGRESS TOWARD LIFE-SAVING CURES
YES on 38 will ensure California universities and nonprofit research institutions can continue vitally needed immunology research to cure and prevent the most debilitating diseases.
“Immunology saved my life-I now live cancer-free, and it could save millions of other lives too.”
-Andrew Dale, Immunotherapy Patient and Cancer Survivor
YES ON 38 IS DESIGNED TO PAY FOR ITSELF-WITH NO COST TO TAXPAYERS
Ten percent (10%) of revenue from licensing immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset bond costs. These requirements are locked into this measure.
YES ON 38 MANDATES STRONG ACCOUNTABILITY & TRANSPARENCY
2% Cap on State Administrative Expenses
Public Disclosure of Spending
Independent Financial Audits
YES ON 38 LOWERS HEALTHCARE COSTS
Immunotherapies developed through Prop. 38 must be provided to California patients at 20% discount. Preventing and curing diseases will also save families and the state billions of dollars in long-term healthcare expenses.
DOCTORS, NURSES AND PATIENT ADVOCATES URGE YES ON 38
• Alzheimer’s Association • American Nurses Association\ California • ALS Association • Kidney Cancer Association • Melanoma Research Alliance • National Multiple Sclerosis Society • The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research ... and many more.
Support Life-Saving Cures. Please Vote YES on 38.
www.YESon38.com
Andrew Dale , Cancer Survivor
Santa Monica
Anne M. Holloway , Board Member
The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research
Chris Tarver , R.N., President
American Nurses Association\California

assistantMessageEvent.content:
The official guide's case against it reads as mild and academic, and it barely raises the self-dealing issue, which is weak opposition in the material most voters will actually see. The pro side, backed by patient advocacy groups, comes across as the more emotionally persuasive one. Overall it looks like "Yes" has the edge. Before settling on that, I want to check whether anything could flip it, like the partisan split in the September PPIC poll.

I'm checking the partisan breakdown: Republicans went from opposed in September to 37% yes in October, while Democrats slipped from 76% to 70%, a net gain of two for yes. I'm also noting that no other Prop 38 polls appear in the tracker, and I'm weighing whether a late swing toward No could still overturn a 16-point lead with only 2% undecided.

The later-November turnout and the 2024 bond results still point toward yes, with a roughly 80% estimate. A "billionaire" backlash could hurt the measure, but Prop 40 trailing suggests voters aren't strongly anti-billionaire. Stacking it beside the housing bonds raises some worry about "too much debt," though the 2024 precedent of two large bonds passing together argues against that.

**yes**

The election hadn't been decided when I checked. Every results page I found, including AP, the Secretary of State and The Ballot Book, still showed "awaiting results." So this is a forecast. I'd put the chance that Prop 38 passes at roughly 80%.

- **Polling:** PPIC is the only public pollster that asked about Prop 38. Its October 16–22 survey of likely voters had it ahead 57% to 41%, up from 55% to 42% in September. In past November elections, PPIC's late bond numbers were close or came in under the result. In 2024, Prop 2 polled 52% and got 58.6%, and Prop 4 polled 60% and got 59.8%. Its big misses ran the other way, but in March primaries: 2024's Prop 1 polled 59% and passed with only 50.2%.
- **Money:** The Yes side reported about $71 million in contributions through October 22, almost all from Gary Michelson. The No side reported about $12,000 and ran no paid ads.
- **Endorsements:** Both the state Democratic and Republican parties back it, as does Governor Newsom, along with patient groups like the Alzheimer's Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation and nurses' associations. Opponents include nearly every major newspaper editorial board, the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the DSA and Tom Steyer.
- **Betting markets:** On the night of November 2, Kalshi had it at about 89% to pass and Polymarket at about 72%.
- **Precedent:** California voters have approved both earlier medical-research bonds: Prop 71 (stem cells, 2004) with 59%, and Prop 14 (stem cells, 2020) with 51% despite having less money behind it.

**What could flip it:** Press coverage has hammered the fact that half the $8.4 billion is written so only Michelson's own institute qualifies. CalMatters reported in October that the institute had just three employees. Voters are also gloomy about the economy, and late-deciding voters tend to break against bonds. For No to win, though, support would need to fall about 8 points from the last poll.

YES

NO

I'm looking at Prop 38 on the November 3, 2026 California ballot, which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half of that would go to a single UC-affiliated nonprofit research institute, and I'm trying to figure out which institute that might be. Next I'll look into the details.

Next I'm weighing the odds: California bond measures have usually passed, including the stem cell bonds in 2004 and 2020, though this one targets a single institute. The opposition argument is thin, with only one signatory, and the backers include several patient and health groups. I want to find out who is behind the measure and whether any polling exists, and I'll also check what else is on the November 2026 ballot, since a crowded list can affect how voters treat bonds.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures- Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)- giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Among the groups, Democrats slipped from 76% to 70% support, Republicans rose from 23% to 37%, and independents stayed about even, which nudged the overall figure from 55 to 57. A California proposition to fund medical research is creating strange alliances on both sides
By Kathryn Palmer (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/kathryn-palmer/) , Staff Writer Oct 15, 2026
Scientists from UCSF, UC Berkeley and Stanford, community members and state Sen. Scott Wiener rally in San Francisco on May 16, 2025 to support a ballot measure to offset scientific research cuts. That measure will appear on the 2028 ballot.
Jessica Christian/S.F. Chronicle
A ballot measure that would raise billions for health research is drawing some unlikely foes, in a race that has already forged a handful of atypical alliances.
Proposition 38 would authorize the state to borrow $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, presented as a way of backfilling some of the widespread cuts to federal research funding by President Donald Trump.
The funds would be split between an unnamed University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for public or nonprofit research institutions, and half of the funds are earmarked to support research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s.

But the measure’s cast of supporters and detractors are not quite so clear-cut.
On the Yes on Prop 38 side, California’s Republican and Democratic parties are in rare agreement, both backing a yes vote on the billion-dollar bond measure.
Gov. Gavin Newsom also said he plans to vote for the measure in November (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), joining a list of health and research advocacy groups including the Parkinson’s Foundation, the ALS Association and the American Nurses Association of California.
On the opposite side, the No on Prop 38 campaign has amassed its own eclectic — albeit much smaller — group of backers. The progressive League of Women Voters of California and Common Cause California find themselves in rare company with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a conservative-aligned anti-tax group that opposes virtually every bond measure.

Article continues below this ad
And this week, the measure attracted a new front of opposition from a trio of current and former California state parks professionals and officials.
That might prompt a reasonable question: What do parks even have to do with a health bond?
Ruth Coleman, executive director of trade organization California Parks Hospitality Association, joined the No on Prop 38 campaign to decry the ballot measure’s possible impacts on other state funding priorities, including public parks.
“Any measure that increases our bonded indebtedness increases pressure on programs like state parks,” Coleman said at a Tuesday news conference.
Coleman is a former director of California State Parks and a former fiscal analyst in the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state’s nonpartisan fiscal and policy analysis organization. She warned that because the bond’s repayment takes priority, it could cut into the state’s ability to pay for other programs in leaner years.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the measure will cost the state $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years in bond repayment.
Coleman clarified she doesn’t think that bonds themselves are bad, and that they have helped fund public parks in recent years. She and two other former parks professionals, however, warned that funding for public spaces could fall on the cutting room floor if the bond passes. In economic downturns, Coleman said legislators have looked at parks funding as “a nice to have, but not a must have.”
In 2024, California voters approved Prop 4 to authorize $10 billion in bonds for projects to reduce climate risks and impacts, and committed $190 million to the statewide parks program.
As of Wednesday, the No campaign did not count any organizations representing parks, conservation or the environment among its backers.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on 38 campaign, said in a statement that the ballot measure would not compete with other priorities, as it is “designed to pay for itself.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 requires that the institutes receiving the funds try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research, and that 10% of any related revenues go to the state. According to a report by the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, that potential revenue source is uncertain, and dependent on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments, and how successful they are.
Researchers from Doudna Labs discussed the ramifications of National Institutes of Health research cuts with members of Congress in Berkeley on Feb. 21, 2025.
Colin Peck/For the S.F. Chronicle It’s not a new bond structure — two semi-recent ballot measures took similar approaches to scientific research.
In 2004, voters approved Prop 71, a $3 billion bond measure to fund stem cell therapy research with the aim of bolstering critical studies and therapies for rare and complex diseases. A 2018 investigation by the Chronicle (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/) found the measure failed to reach its promises of paying the state back in billions of discovery-related royalties.
In 2020, voters approved Prop 14 to infuse another $5.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research.

Article continues below this ad
Swanson said Prop 38 will provide billions in “vitally needed funding to advance breakthrough immunology research to develop life-saving treatments and cures for the most persistent and debilitating diseases.”
The measure has sparked criticism for its hyper-specific language that appears to ensure half the billion-dollar funds go directly to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy, the sole institution that meets the measure’s criteria. The ballot measure’s proponent and largest financial backer, philanthropist Gary Michelson, is a co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
The opposition camp is headed by Robert Kaplan, a senior scholar at the Clinical Excellence Research Center at Stanford School of Medicine and David Panush, a veteran legislative adviser and president of consulting firm California Health Policy Strategies. They object to the use of bond funds to support scientific research rather than general budgeting processes, and criticize it as inflexible and lacking transparency.
Panush has called the measure an outrageous attempt to use the ballot initiative process to fund Michelson’s institute. The California chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America made the same point to explain its opposition, calling the measure “naked self-dealing” in its voter guide.
Just a few weeks out from the Nov. 3 election, the Yes on 38 campaign’s coffers sit at a dramatic advantage, outraising the opposition campaign by the millions. Bolstered by multiple million-dollar contributions by Michelson, the Yes campaign boasts more than $50 million raised, while the No campaign hasn’t yet topped the $10,000 mark as of Wednesday.
The controversial requirements stand in stark contrast with a competing science bond ballot measure that failed to secure a spot on the November ballot.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, introduced Senate Bill 895 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) in the first few weeks of the legislative session, which began as a $23 billion bond measure designed to backfill Trump cuts to science and health research. After months of debate and a significant slash down to $12 billion, the measure appeared poised for the November ballot. But in obscure last-minute negotiations involving top Democratic leadership and the governor’s office, it was punted to 2028. The bond amount was also cut down even further, to $7.5 billion.
In his ballot statement, Kaplan pointed to Wiener’s bond as a better alternative to Prop 38, which proposes creating a new state agency to distribute and manage the funds, and would be able to meet changing funding and research needs rather than committing the funds to specific institutions and research areas indefinitely.
Erik Mebust, spokesperson for Wiener, said he is not taking a position on Prop 38.
Trump last year froze more than $600 million to fund UC research that a judge eventually restored months later. The National Institutes of Health under Trump also scaled back the number of new research grants it funded in 2025 to 3,900 from 5,000 the year before under President Joe Biden.
Grants for Alzheimer’s disease research were cut in half and new cancer research grants dropped by 23%, according to federal data.

I'm going through the endorsements for Prop 38. Most of the newspapers, including the Bay Area News Group, Press-Enterprise, OC Register, Sacramento Bee, San Diego Union-Tribune, SF Bay Guardian, SF Chronicle, and probably Santa Rosa Press-Democrat, are against it, while the LA Times has no endorsement. On the non-profit side, California Church IMPACT is for it, and the California Pan-Ethnic Health Network is against it, with CalTax still to check.

Both major parties back it, while every major newspaper opposes it. The yes side has a large money edge and PPIC polling sits at 57-41, which points toward passage. I'm also weighing how past measures with that kind of spending and editorial opposition have fared, and how the crowded ballot might affect voters.

I'm checking the earlier polling comparisons: the late PPIC numbers for past bond measures, and whether those polls tended to overstate or understate final support.

I'm now checking how PPIC's late polls for earlier bond measures compared with final results. Prop 13 in 2020 and the 2018 bonds like Props 1, 2, 3, and 4 show polls sometimes landing close to the result and sometimes well off, so I'm noting where the gaps were largest.

I'm weighing PPIC's 57-41 lead against typical late shifts toward "no," which would still leave it passing around 52-54%. I also want to check for other polls from late October and any post-election results, since the page may have been fetched before those came out.

I'm now looking for any post-election coverage of Prop 38, searching for results that might confirm whether voters approved or rejected the immunology bond.

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) This guide covers what the text does, the three research bonds California has already approved or scheduled, the organization the institute criteria describe, the measure's transparency rules, the royalty and discount provisions, the cost, the money behind each side, the arguments and the polling.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."
California has borrowed for medical research twice before and has a third research bond scheduled for 2028:
The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) notes that funding for medical research and development in the United States "totaled about $300 billion in 2023," most of it from companies and the federal government. Common Cause.
Proposition 38 after November 3 would mean bond sales from 2027 or a 2028 vote on the SB 895 research bond instead:
If Prop 38 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the results, which is due December 11. The Department of Public Health would then have 90 days to sign a funding agreement with an institute meeting the seven criteria, the $100 million start-up loan would become available, and the Treasurer could begin selling bonds on the institute's written request. Repayment of $500 million to $600 million a year would begin as bonds are sold and run for about 20 years. If it fails, no immunology bond is authorized, CIRM continues under Proposition 14's authorization, and the next decision on research borrowing comes on March 7, 2028, when SB 895's $7.5 billion bond goes to voters. Either way, that 2028 vote is already scheduled.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, campaign-finance data as of October 14, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), the institute's tax filing for the year ending June 30, 2025, party and gubernatorial positions as of October 17, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–10, 2026.

I'm recalling PPIC's October 2024 ballot measure numbers from memory, comparing their yes shares against the actual results. Several of those figures I'm not certain of, so I'm checking which measures they tended to overstate.

I'm now trying to recall PPIC's February 2024 numbers on Prop 1 and whether polls overstated the yes side there, though I'm not sure of the exact figures. Next I'm checking whether there was a public poll on Prop 14 in November 2020.

I'm checking whether PPIC's October 2020 survey or the Berkeley IGS September 2020 poll covered Prop 14, and whether SurveyUSA did. For Prop 38, the 57-41 PPIC lead is worth weighing against typical late erosion, since opposition has spent only about $12K, so paid counter-messaging is minimal.

I'm listing California citizen-initiated bond measures from past years to see how they fared, noting that the 2018 water bond failed narrowly after drawing some environmental opposition.

I'm trying to recall whether PPIC polled the 2018 water bond, Prop 3, in October, and what it showed, though I'm not confident of the numbers. I'll look up a PPIC October 2018 Prop 3 result to calibrate against.

I'm weighing the odds that Prop 38 passes: PPIC's 57-41 lead is large, and the measure has heavy funding behind it with little organized opposition. I'm also thinking about whether the current mood toward debt, with inflation and tight household budgets, could erode that margin, since Prop 38 is the lowest of the three bond measures PPIC tested.

I'm weighing a probability of about 75-85% that Prop 38 passes, given the large lead and heavy funding, but I'm wondering whether voters reading the ballot label, which names a single UC-affiliated institute, might turn against it late. I'm looking at how accurate PPIC's past bond polling has been, and checking for any late news such as a scandal, lawsuit, or attorney general inquiry involving the institute, by searching for coverage of CIII and the Prop 38 lawsuit.

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/)
October 20, 2026 October 20, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)

Courtyard view of the UCLA Research Park under construction in the former Westside Pavilion shopping center in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024. Photo by Brian van der Brug, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
READ NEXT
This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/)
July 31, 2026 August 3, 2026
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
